title: Pick an Index by Weight
statement:
Build a picker that chooses an index at random, where heavier indexes come up more often.

  • WeightedPicker(weights) receives positive whole numbers; weights[i] is the weight of index i.
  • pick() returns an index i with probability weights[i] / sum(weights). Each call is independent of the others.

With weights = [1, 3], index 0 should come up about a quarter of the time and index 1 about three quarters.

The output is random, so it is not compared exactly. The checker verifies that every result is a valid index and that, over many calls, each index appears about as often as its weight says. Tests are a list of operations; the first one creates the picker, and the output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: With a single index, every pick must return 0.
Index 1 holds 3 of the 4 units of weight, so it should win about 75% of picks. Any sequence of 0s and 1s is possible in a short run.

hints: Lay the weights end to end on a number line of length sum(weights). Index i owns a segment as long as its weight.
Draw a random point on that line. Which segment it lands in is your answer. How do you describe where each segment ends?
Store prefix sums. Draw an integer target in [1, total] and binary-search the first prefix sum that is ≥ target.

explain.intuition:
Picture the weights as strips laid end to end: index 0 covers [0, w0), index 1 covers [w0, w0 + w1), and so on. A uniformly random point on the whole line lands in strip i with probability equal to its length over the total, which is exactly the weight rule.

The strip ends are the prefix sums, and they are sorted because every weight is positive. So finding the strip that contains the point is a binary search for the first prefix sum greater than the point. The constructor does the O(n) work once; every pick is O(log n). This is how weighted A/B test buckets or ad rotation are often done.
steps: In the constructor, build prefix[i] = weights[0] + … + weights[i] and remember total = prefix[n − 1].
In pick, draw a random real x in [0, total).
pitfalls: Off-by-one at the strip edges: drawing an integer in [0, total − 1] but searching for prefix[i] ≥ x gives index 0 one extra unit of weight and starves the last one.
Building the prefix sums inside pick, which makes every call O(n).
Expanding each index into weights[i] copies in a big array. It works, but the array can hold a billion entries.

complexity.time: O(n) to build, O(log n) per pick

solutions.title: Prefix sums and a linear scan
solutions.idea: Draw a point on the line of total weight and walk the prefix sums until one passes it.

solutions.title: Prefix sums and binary search
solutions.idea: The prefix sums are sorted, so the strip containing a random point is found by binary search.
solutions.time: O(n) to build, O(log n) per pick

followups: Weights change between picks (update one weight at a time). Which structure keeps both updates and picks O(log n)?
Make pick O(1) after an O(n) setup. (Look up the alias method.)
